The AI placebo effect, whereby the mere belief in artificial intelligence assistance alters userexpectations and task performance, is an established phenomenon in human-computer interaction(HCI). Yet the cognitive mechanisms linking placebo beliefs to objective behavioural outcomes remainpoorly understood. This study applies a hierarchical Bayesian computational framework to re-analysedata from Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzletask under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AIassistance). We compared three models in which the AI placebo manipulation altered either (a) themean of a prior performance expectation distribution (Shift model), (b) the precision (inverse variance)of that distribution (Precision model), or (c) both simultaneously (Combined model). Bayesian modelcomparison via Leave-One-Out cross-validation strongly favoured the Combined model(elpd_diff = 7.11 over the next-best model). Despite the winning model, group-level analyses revealedno statistically reliable average shift in either prior mean or precision due to the placebo manipulation(95% HDIs broadly overlapping zero), mirroring the null group-level performance effect reported byKosch et al. Crucially, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean shift was stronglyand positively correlated with observed performance improvement (r = 0.973, p < .0001), explaining theindividual-level expectancy–performance relationship originally observed. Unexpectedly, reduced priorprecision (not increased precision) was associated with greater performance gains under the placebo(r = 0.595, p < .0001). These findings provide the first demonstration that hierarchical Bayesian modelsoriginally developed to explain placebo analgesia can successfully account for individual differences inthe AI placebo effect on objective task performance. The results indicate that the cognitive mechanisminvolves simultaneous modulation of both expectation level and expectation certainty, yet manifestshighly heterogeneously across participants. We discuss implications for theories of expectancy-drivenperformance and for HCI evaluation methodology.

Peptides are among the smallest functional biomolecules. Learning to systematically design their activity would revolutionize biology and medicine. Yet achieving this goal remains an open challenge. Recent advances in machine learning enable the discovery and design of peptides at scale, not only yielding new antibiotic agents effective against priority pathogens but also revealing unexpected roles for peptides in host immunity. In this review, we survey how artificial intelligence (AI) methods can be used to mine genomes, proteomes, and even ancient sequence data to uncover “encrypted” peptide antibiotics across the tree of life and over evolutionary time. We highlight emerging approaches for activity prediction, structure–activity modeling, sequence optimization, and de novo peptide generation, and we discuss workflows that tightly couple in silico design with high-throughput experimental validation. We further introduce the concept of “encrypted immunity,” in which ordinary proteins encode latent antimicrobial fragments, and we outline translational opportunities as well as remaining challenges on the path to bringing AI-designed peptides to the clinic.

Data-driven battery prognostics can fail when models trained on one chemistry are deployed on another. This study investigates early-life end-of-life (EOL) classification under chemistry-driven domain shift and introduces a schema-constrained large language model (LLM) configuration layer as the primary methodological contribution. The LLM does not predict EOL directly and does not introduce a new transfer-learning or uncertainty-estimation algorithm. Instead, it maps structured chemistry context and numerical dataset evidence to an executable architecture, reliability head, and bounded set of training hyperparameters selected from an approved model zoo containing one-dimensional CNN, self-attention, WideResNet, OpenMax, and Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) options. Full degradation trajectories define five EOL categories using an 80% state-of-health threshold, whereas model inputs are restricted to early-cycle observations. Across six directed Argonne/CAMP chemistry-transfer tasks, the target-only deterministic CNN achieved a mean balanced accuracy of 68.9%, compared with 78.3% for the LLM-selected CNN with self-attention and SNGP, corresponding to an average improvement of 9.4 percentage points. Fixed non-LLM transfer alternatives achieved 70.0% for the deterministic CNN, 71.7% for the OpenMax-enforced CNN, 66.5% for deterministic WideResNet, and 73.3% for WideResNet-SNGP. Context ablation further reduced LLM-selected accuracy from 78.3% with history and chemistry context to 73.5% without history, 71.6% without chemistry, and 67.1% when both were removed. These results support the use of constrained LLM guidance as an auditable configuration-selection layer, while cross-chemistry transfer learning and uncertainty-aware EOL prediction provide the experimental setting in which that selection mechanism is evaluated.

Generative artificial intelligence is promoted as a way of tailoring instruction to learners, yet most reported applications stay within language and general-education settings, and few measure outcomes in courses whose value lies in design and production skill. This paper describes a four-module generative AI framework for resource development that links learner and content modelling, generation, assessment and community iteration to a course-grounded knowledge base, with the teacher reviewing before release. It was evaluated in a twelve-week quasi-experiment in a professional core course, Micro-lecture Design and Production, at a Chinese vocational college. Two intact classes (n = 45, 44) were taught by the same instructor, who designed the framework; assignment was not random. Covariance-adjusted posttest means differed by 5.6 points (82.3 versus 76.7, p < .001, partial η² = .24), and the framework-supported class reported higher motivation and satisfaction; self-directed learning differed modestly. Preparation time per unit fell by half, though the work became more concentrated and the knowledge base carried a large one-off cost. Because the design cannot separate the framework from the additional resources it produced, the results are framed as associations rather than effects.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Jean Piaget’s constructivist theory emphasizes active knowledge construction, yet its application in Indonesian Islamic Boarding Schools (IIBS) remains limited. This phenomenological case study examines how constructivist principles are integrated into IIBS English lesson plans using a critical discourse analysis approach. Seven lesson plans from an IIBS in East Java were analyzed over six months. Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis (CDA) was employed to examine power dynamics and ideological influences in classroom discourse within the lesson plans. Findings revealed that while constructivist elements such as problem-based learning, collaborative discussions, and metacognitive reflection are present, their implementation is constrained by hierarchical teacher-student relationships and religious-nationalist discourse framing. Lesson plans encourage active engagement but often reinforce predefined moral and ideological narratives, limiting opportunities for critical inquiry and independent knowledge construction. Despite this, Piagetian principles align with certain Islamic educational traditions, such as ijtihad (independent reasoning) and shura (consultative learning), providing potential avenues for deeper cognitive engagement. This study empirically contributes to qualitative evidence on how Piaget’s constructivist theory is applied within IIBS. This study also offers a practical hybrid pedagogical approach that combines experiential learning with structured guidance, fostering critical thinking without disrupting Islamic traditions.

EEG foundation models report downstream gains, yet their protocols seldom include three controls. These are the same encoder untrained, spectral features fitted on the same data, and a layer picked without looking at test scores. We therefore evaluate five publicly released EEG foundation models and an in-house JEPA-style model under one protocol with all three controls and several seeds, on five benchmarks and four added task families. The controls change the reading in three ways. First, picking the probed layer by its test score raises the layer-wise peak by an average of +0.034 and reverses the peak-versus-output gap in 9 of 36 cells. Second, with the layer picked on validation, random initialisation matches or beats pretraining for half of the models on sleep and emotion, and no model beats a five-band log-power baseline on emotion or motor imagery. Third, after full fine-tuning only 5 of 30 pairs gain beyond twice their seed spread, and the one clear loss of -0.290 AUROC persists under matched learning rates. From these results we draw four reporting practices, and we release every cell for re-analysis.

This study examined associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty in the use of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for Indonesian e-commerce. A cross-sectional survey collected questionnaire responses from 300 purposively selected consumers who had experience with e-commerce chatbots or virtual assistants. The analysis used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 to assess 18 indicators across three reflective constructs. The reported measurement properties met the specified reliability and validity thresholds. The reported PLS-SEM results indicated positive direct associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty, alongside a positive specific indirect association through Perceived Empathy. However, discrepancies between the structural model and the direct-effects table prevent a definitive interpretation of the estimated effect magnitudes and mediation type. However, coefficients in the structural diagram differed from those in the direct-effects table, so the magnitudes and type of mediation could not be confirmed from the reported outputs. The study distinguishes perceived conversational naturalness from perceived understanding and company-directed loyalty intentions. These findings concern self-reported perceptions and intentions rather than observed repurchase behavior. Its cross-sectional design and purposive sample preclude causal conclusions and population-wide generalization. The results provide a basis for evaluating interaction quality and perceived understanding in chatbot-supported customer service.

Working with people requires making thousands of decisions every day—with little help, less time, and often no context. Customer service providers are constantly determining how to respond, what to prioritize, and when to act. The quality of those decisions depends on one’s ability to think critically, reflect thoughtfully, and choose decisively. This chapter examines what research reveals about finding the right balance between reflection and action—when to pause and when to decide, and what questions to ask. It then transitions into decision-making as a structured process, arguing that a good decision isn’t necessarily one with a perfect outcome, but one made through clear reasoning and balanced consideration. Readers will learn to evaluate choices by weighing the long-term benefits, the short-term costs, and the greater good. In its final section, the chapter introduces the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing decision-making. Rather than replacing human judgment, AI serves as a thought partner—helping service providers identify blind spots, test assumptions, and explore alternative viewpoints. Throughout the book, readers will find AI reflection prompts and decision.

In today's digital workplace, employment decisions are increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI) and social media platforms, embedding societal biases into managerial practices and undermining traditional legal safeguards. This article introduces the concept of crowd discrimination, which arises when biases originating from customers, algorithms, or online communities influence employment outcomes, thus threatening workers' right to equality. Specifically, it argues that platform-based work, AI-driven management tools, and online shaming systematically transform crowd biases into employment decisions regarding hiring, dismissal, wages, and working conditions. Crowd discrimination is not incidental. It results from both technological design and the limitations of existing laws, which fail to adequately address these new discriminatory practices. Employers utilize AI and platform infrastructures, whether intentionally or not, to distance their decisions from discriminatory effects, thereby evading legal accountability. Meanwhile, platform and AI companies shape employment conditions through their technologies without recognized legal responsibility, complicating employers' obligations under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and obscuring the sources of discrimination. To address these challenges, the article calls for new legal duties to protect workplace equality. It proposes procedural protections enabling workers to enforce equality rights, particularly in cases mediated by AI systems and platforms. Further, it argues for imposing direct liability on platform and AI companies whose technologies facilitate discrimination, whether through embedding biased patterns into AI tools or allowing customer preferences to dictate employment outcomes. By adopting this broader legal approach, the article offers a comprehensive framework to address the threats crowd discrimination poses to workplace equality.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a modified cumulative damage sequential preventive maintenance (CDSPM) model that addresses the limitations of traditional cumulative shock sequential models by incorporating three realistic factors often ignored in maintenance planning: prior damage in used machines, shock dampening effects and non-constant shock magnitudes. The research seeks to provide a more practical decision-making tool for industries, particularly in developing countries, that rely heavily on fairly-used equipment exposed to complex shock environments. Design/methodology/approach The study modifies the existing CDSPM model by introducing a non-zero initial damage state (R0 > 0), a shock dampening factor αl which is defined as the proportion of shock damage absorbed by the machine. This provides a mathematical mechanism for representing the protective effect of built-in shock-resistance components. The effective shock damage transmitted to the machine is represented by 1-αl100% with 0⩽αl⩽1. This formulation distinguishes between the physical magnitude of an external shock and the actual damage transmitted to the machine. It therefore provides a theoretical basis for incorporating mechanical protection into stochastic reliability models rather than assuming that the entire shock magnitude contributes directly to cumulative damage. Also, the Gamma-distributed shock magnitudes replace the traditional exponential distribution. The modified model formulates total expected cost functions for both infinite and finite time horizons, derives optimality conditions using Lagrange optimization, and develops a comprehensive availability model. The methodology is validated through application to a used Caterpillar 320BL hydraulic excavator using empirical field data, with the algorithm implemented in Python programming language. Findings The modified CDSPM model demonstrates that accounting for prior damage and shock resistance leads to shorter, effective and more realistic maintenance intervals with lower expected maximum cost rate compared to classical models. The optimal policy recommends P* = 12 maintenance intervals with a maximum expected cost rate of 26.99 million Naira and system availability of 98.51%, whereas the classical model (assuming pristine condition) suggests P** = 14 intervals with 58.98 million Naira cost and 99.18% availability for the case study used Caterpillar excavator. The 15% reduction in intervals and significantly lower lifecycle costs confirm the fact that classical models overestimate equipment longevity and underestimate maintenance requirements for fairly-used machines. Research limitations/implications The model's parameters are estimated from a single machine type and operational context, which may limit generalizability. The assumption of a constant shock dampening factor and fixed improvement factor may not capture all operational complexities. These identified baseline conditions are essential for real-world model development. Therefore, future research should explore time-varying dampening factors, multiple failure mechanisms and application to diverse equipment types across different industrial sectors. Practical implications The modified CDSPM model provides maintenance planners with a practical tool for scheduling sequential preventive maintenance (PM) on used equipment, enabling more accurate prediction of maintenance intervals, cost optimization and availability estimation that could not have been appropriate with fixed interval PM. The approach helps reduce unplanned failures, minimize downtime and extend equipment life through evidence-based decision-making that reflects actual machine conditions. Social implications By improving cumulative damage sequential maintenance practices for fairly-used equipment, particularly in developing countries where second-hand machinery is prevalent, the model supports sustainable industrial operations, reduces resource waste and enhances productivity and workers' safety through more reliable equipment performance. This cost-effective maintenance strategy contributes to economic efficiency in resource-constrained environments. Originality/value This research presents an integrated CDSPM model that simultaneously incorporates prior damage, shock dampening and Gamma-distributed shock magnitudes. The work extends Nakagawa and Mizutani’s (2008) foundational model as a special case while providing a more realistic model for used equipment maintenance. The availability model and finite horizon optimization approach offer novel contributions to reliability engineering practice.

The digital age has seen the sophistication of cyber-attacks increase faster than conventional security control measures, requiring novel and intelligent defense systems. Next-generation cybersecurity incorporates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in order to enhance computer security with automation, flexibility, and real-time detection of threats. AI-enabled systems are able to run large volumes of data, learn deviations, discover zero-day vulnerabilities, and handle cyber threats with limited human oversight. These smart models keep on learning through the changing patterns of attacks and improve the accuracy and speed with which intrusion detection is done, and reduce the false positives. Artificial intelligence has a role in digital forensics in the automated recovery of data, evidence gathering, and behavior analysis to assist investigators in tracking the digital footprint and creating cybercrime incidents with high accuracy. More complex tools like Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Deep Learning can also be used to detect the unseen links between networks of cybercrime. Nevertheless, AI-driven cybersecurity implementation results in issues of data privacy, the transparency of the algorithms, and the possible abuse of AI by ill-intentioned individuals. The solution to these issues should be a balanced solution that involves a combination of human and smart systems to guarantee ethical and trustworthy safety. In general, AI in cybersecurity and forensics symbolizes a disruptive step to the predictive, self-sufficient, and resilient architecture of defense, and the future of a safer and more reliable online system.

Decision-relevant building damage assessment is critical for prioritizing resources and recovery after a disaster. Most automated methods, however, either flatten damage into a single severity scale (no damage, minor, major, destroyed) or require paired pre- and post-event imagery that is often unavailable for emerging hazards. This paper presents Damage-TriageFormer, a single-image, post-event, footprint-conditioned model that produces a damage typology rather than a severity scale. We make two contributions. First, DamageTriage-Bench combines NOAA Emergency Response Imagery from Hurricane Michael (2018), Hurricane Helene (2024), and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfire complex with five typology classes that distinguish roof from structural damage and partial from total extent. Its photo-atomic splits keep all tiles from a source photo in one fold. Second, Damage-TriageFormer pairs a DINOv3 ViT-L backbone with a two-stage gated damage head and an auxiliary severity objective under building-footprint conditioning. Across three training seeds, its crop-conditioned configuration reaches mean macro F1 of 0.662 on validation and 0.620 on the held-out test fold. Controlled experiments associate this performance with the crop training recipe as a whole, which differs from the recipe of the tile-level variant in the trainable layers, learning rates, logit adjustment, weight averaging, and schedule: training the same crops with the tile-level recipe lowers test macro F1 by 0.067, whereas the head variants and the effective input resolution of the crops show no statistically distinguishable differences. The model is most accurate on the two visually distinct endpoint classes, with mean test F1 of 0.92 on undamaged buildings and 0.85 on total structural collapse. The aggregate expected calibration error of the seed-42 checkpoint is 0.016, but class-conditional analysis shows that its rare-class predictions are overconfident. While the rare Total Roof Damage class remains difficult, consistent with its limited examples and an ambiguous label boundary, the results show that single-image post-event imagery contains useful signal for building damage typing without a pre-event reference. Field use would still require external validation, reliable footprint data, and human inspection.

This study examines the evolution of research on data analytics in management accounting by identifying publication trends, influential contributors, collaboration networks, and emerging research themes. Using bibliometric methods, including performance analysis and science mapping, the study analyzes 129 articles published in Scopus-indexed journals between 2014 and 2025. The findings show that the literature is primarily centered on accounting information systems, big data, and artificial intelligence, while machine learning, blockchain technology, and cloud computing have emerged as significant directions for future investigation. By mapping the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this research domain, the study provides a comprehensive overview of existing knowledge, identifies key research gaps, and proposes an integrative agenda for future research. These findings offer useful insights for both researchers and practitioners seeking to advance the application of data analytics in management accounting.

This meta-research study will assess the availability and FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of data supporting the primary outcomes of intervention studies on oral mucositis in children and adolescents (0–19 years). Oral mucositis is a painful and common complication of chemotherapy, head and neck radiotherapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation conditioning. It can affect eating, speaking, infection risk, and cancer treatment itself. Data sharing in dentistry has been shown to be rare, but no study has yet assessed it in pediatric oral mucositis research specifically. We will run a systematic search, with no language or date restrictions, of MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses. We will include prospective intervention studies, randomized or non-randomized, in which at least one primary outcome relates to oral mucositis. Screening, data extraction, and all assessments will be performed independently by one human reviewer and a generative AI tool (Claude, Anthropic) acting as second reviewer, with disagreements resolved by a third human reviewer. For each study, we will classify both declared and effective data availability, including the data availability statement, access route, repository, identifier, license, and documentation. When data are "available on request," we will contact the authors in a standardized way. We will assess located datasets that have a persistent identifier or resolvable URL using the automated F-UJI tool. Risk of bias (RoB 2 / ROBINS-I) and discrepancies between registered and reported primary outcomes will be explored as secondary aims. The study will not synthesize clinical effects. We expect to estimate the proportion of studies with complete, partial, or no effective data availability and to describe the FAIRness levels of the datasets we locate, including differences between publication periods (up to 2015 vs. 2016 onward). The findings should show where data transparency and responsible reuse can be improved in pediatric oral mucositis research.

Abstract: Title: L0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM): A Deterministic Control Architecture for Critical L0 Infrastructure and Boundary-Constrained Systems Abstract:The increasing reliance on probabilistic Artificial Intelligence and continuous floating-point algorithms in Operational Technology (OT) and Level 0 (L0) critical infrastructure introduces unacceptable risks of stochastic drift, computational latency, and unpredictable edge-case failures. Drawing from the historical transition from additive, zero-less Roman numerals to positional Arabic numerals, this paper argues that modern AI suffers from a structural "Roman Matrix Bloat"—attempting to solve physical control problems by infinitely scaling parameter spaces rather than anchoring value to position and structural equilibrium. To eliminate unconstrained floating-point infinities, we introduce the **L0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM)** architecture—a fundamentally deterministic control paradigm based on discrete positional geometry and axiomatic teleology. The L0-ISM framework maps multidimensional physical and operational parameters onto a rigid, symmetric discrete scale ranging from -9 to +9 using unique, non-repeating positional digits (from 0 to 9), where 0 represents absolute thermodynamic or logical equilibrium (the fulcrum of a balance scale). System states are encapsulated as finite k-dimensional tuples and routed through precompiled Lookup Tables operating in constant time O(1), entirely eliminating computational latency and stochastic uncertainty. The architecture features hardware-level absorbing boundaries at -9 and +9 for immediate interdiction (Hard Stop, -999) and integrates input hysteresis alongside temporal gradients to ensure physical stability against signal noise and actuator chatter. Furthermore, because the state space is strictly bounded to a finite set of 19^k states, the entire logic matrix is natively compatible with exhaustive formal mathematical verification via SMT solvers (such as Z3), guaranteeing the absolute absence of critical failure paths. As documented in early archival records and exploratory working files, the architecture underwent a real-time documented evolution—from early conceptual drafts (Invariant Bytes) to a unified, multi-domain engineering standard. Validated across applications ranging from high-density AI data center liquid cooling (mCDU) to offline transactional edge nodes (Store and Forward T-OTP protocols), the L0-ISM architecture provides a zero-hallucination, fault-tolerant execution engine designed for physical environments where operational failure is simply not an option.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can read startup pitch decks, but letting them emit investment scores directly invites score inflation, run-to-run variance and rationales that are hard to audit. We describe DealsFlow, a human-in-the-loop agentic harness deployed at a UK early-stage fund. The LLM reads the deck, cites evidence and rates each category; code combines the ratings, caps them and only ever lowers them. Three mechanisms implement this: a stage-aware corroboration ceiling (78, 70 or 60 out of 100) on factual categories without external evidence; a sceptic call that may lower but never raise a score; and a pre-fetch pattern that retrieves and indexes all evidence before a single generation pass. We evaluate on $N=243$ SEIS/EIS investments with recorded outcomes. Because recent investments have unresolved outcomes, we use the 142 that are at least three years old. There, the full pipeline's score has Spearman $ρ=0.45$ (95% CI 0.32 to 0.57) with the total-value multiple and AUC 0.71 for identifying write-offs, against $ρ=0.38$ and AUC 0.68 for an unconstrained LLM. The gain is small and comes mostly from the sceptic call; we did not test whether its lower-only rule matters. Investments that later exceeded $2\times$ had 64% of factual categories corroborated, against 38% for write-offs (omnibus Kruskal-Wallis test over five outcome groups, $p=0.031$), and our retrieval was not date-restricted, so these figures may overstate screening skill. In a study of 20 inbound applications, analyst time per application fell from 44.7 to 18.9 minutes including verification and correction, and 84% of 240 cited claims were fully supported by their sources, but 70% of reports needed at least one correction.

Health misinformation threatens public health, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a novel tool for correcting it. Its effectiveness and underlying psychological mechanisms, however, remain underexplored. This study compared generative AI-assisted information verification with search-engine-based information verification in reducing public trust in health misinformation and examined the mediating roles of perceived authority and perceived objectivity across two health misinformation topics. Two quasi-experimental pretest-posttest studies were conducted. Experiment 1 (N = 280) targeted the claim that “blood donation is harmful to health,” which centers on alleged physiological risks of donation. Experiment 2 (N = 232) addressed the claim that “hospice care is equivalent to waiting for death,” which concerns perceptions of hospice care, treatment goals, and end-of-life decision-making. Participants were allocated to either a generative AI-assisted or a search-engine-based information verification condition. Trust in health misinformation was measured before and after the information verification task, and perceived authority and perceived objectivity were measured after the task. Analysis of covariance, hierarchical regression, and bootstrap mediation analyses were conducted to test hypotheses. Generative AI-assisted information verification significantly reduced trust in health misinformation in both studies. Mediation analyses showed that perceived authority and perceived objectivity both served as significant mediators. The pattern of hierarchical regression results differed across the two topics: perceived authority showed a more stable association with trust in the blood donation context, whereas perceived objectivity showed a more stable association with trust in the hospice care context. In two quasi-experimental studies, generative AI-assisted information verification was associated with lower trust in the examined health misinformation claims than search-engine-based information verification. The findings suggest that credibility-related evaluations, including perceived authority and perceived objectivity, may help explain the short-term corrective effects of generative AI in health information verification.

This whitepaper analyzes the structural problem of centralization in the development of modern artificial intelligence and proposes a conceptual model of decentralized training based on blockchain technology. It examines how the concentration of data, computational infrastructure and models in a reduced number of global corporations creates technological, economic and strategic dependency worldwide. Through progressive examples—from the basic workings of machine learning to the reuse of computations through hashes—the idea of a distributed network (IAChain) is introduced, in which nodes, data, storage and trainings coexist incentivized through digital tokens. The goal is not to present a finished technical solution, but to open a discussion about the feasibility and potential impact of decentralizing the knowledge and processing that will sustain the next generation of artificial intelligence.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract This viewpoint article argues that South African teacher education requires a distinctly decolonial agenda for generative artificial intelligence (AI), developed in critical dialogue with scholarship from Aotearoa New Zealand and wider international contexts. AI is not a neutral efficiency tool: its infrastructures, training data, evaluation standards, and platform logics can intensify linguistic hierarchy, data extraction, epistemic marginalisation, and pedagogical standardisation. Drawing on epistemic justice, decoloniality, settler-colonial analysis, and wayfinding, the article synthesises policy and scholarship to develop a framework for multilingual, Indigenous, and publicly accountable AI in teacher education. The comparison is deliberately relational rather than transfer-oriented. South Africa and Aotearoa have distinct colonial histories, constitutional arrangements, and Indigenous political formations; nevertheless, Te Tiriti o Waitangi-informed educational thinking, Māori data and algorithmic sovereignty, and Pacific-led teacher education provide productive tests of whether AI governance redistributes authority or merely adds cultural content to externally controlled systems. The article advances six interdependent propositions: language justice by design; Indigenous Knowledge Systems stewardship; critical AI literacy for teacher agency; assessment redesign around process and judgment; public-interest data governance; and infrastructure-aware inclusion. Decolonising AI, it concludes, is not metaphorical branding or the insertion of local examples into imported systems. It requires material changes to curriculum purposes, decision rights, data relations, evaluation criteria, and institutional accountability so that AI strengthens multilingual participation, community authority, teacher judgment, and public benefit.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a primary cause of blindness globally, mostly affecting diabetics. To avoid irreversible vision loss, DR must be identified and classified as early as possible. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) provide promising ways for early identification and grading of DR sets, potentially changing automated retinal image analysis. This review research examines the deep learning models currently in use for the diagnosis and categorization of diabetic retinopathy. It investigates and evaluates the efficacy, accuracy, and efficiency of various machine learning and deep learning architectures, such as ensemble networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and hybrid models, in identifying DR stages from retinal images and samples. The study also examines the datasets that are often used to train and test these models, as well as the issues posed by imbalance, data scarcity, and the requirement for generalization capabilities in the models. It also examines how DL models may be employed in clinical workflows and evaluates how this might improve diagnostic procedures and patient outcomes. By comparing model performances and identifying patterns and gaps in the literature, this research hopes to highlight areas for future development and the potential for DL models to be a cornerstone in DR screening programs. Through extensive research, this study provides academics, medical professionals, and technologists with a clear route forward for the integration of artificial intelligence in ophthalmology, furthering the process toward more exact, effective, and readily accessible DR detection and classification.

The grading of fruits and vegetables is mostly dependent on subjective visual inspection techniques that require labor. Computers and advanced machine learning systems can help to invent non-destructive tools for quality evaluation of fruits and vegetables based on color, size, shape, texture, ripeness, freshness, and surface damage based on computer vision methods. The paper is presenting reviews of methods used for fruit and vegetable grading, including convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, object detection systems, vision transformers, hyperspectral and multimodal vision techniques, and few-shot learning approaches. The review focuses on grading effectiveness, computation complexity, data variety, and algorithms reliability, and it shows that although many studies report the accuracy level higher than 99% while working with particular datasets, most studies used private datasets, making the comparison of results between various studies impossible. In this regard, the paper addresses the issue of a gap between benchmarks and real-life deployment and proposes a framework based on the grading process that includes a confidence lock mechanism for uncertain predictions and a reliable protocol for testing and benchmarking performances of the algorithms This paper lacks any experimental data as the proposed framework and procedures are designed for future assessment.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: This technical report presents a structured taxonomy and research roadmap for deep learning, distinguishing among neural architectures, computational mechanisms, learning paradigms, task-specific architectures, and complete AI systems. The report surveys foundational neural networks, convolutional neural networks, recurrent and sequence-to-sequence architectures, attention mechanisms, Transformer architectures, vision Transformers, generative models, graph deep learning, state-space models, neural differential equations, and deep reinforcement learning. It further examines self-supervised and multimodal learning, mixture-of-experts architectures, meta-learning, continual learning, federated learning, computer vision systems, speech and audio models, time-series modeling, recommendation architectures, metric learning, domain adaptation, knowledge distillation, causal deep learning, neuro-symbolic AI, and emerging neural architectures. The report also covers training and optimization methods, normalization and regularization, large language model efficiency, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, model compression, efficient inference, LLM training and alignment, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic AI, and foundation-model systems. Each major method family is organized around milestone tables, mathematical formulations, and descriptions of its historical development. The report concludes with an overview of the evolution of deep learning, research-oriented mastery levels, and a structured research pathway for natural language processing and large language models. Document type: Technical report / research roadmap Author: Asifur Rahaman

Climate emergencies and generative artificial intelligence are creating new challenges for tourism resilience. Deepfake disaster communication, including AI-generated videos, images, and emergency messages, can spread misinformation, erode trust, distort risk perceptions, and disrupt crisis response. Despite growing research on tourism resilience and crisis communication, limited attention has been given to governance challenges posed by deepfake-driven information disorder during climate-related disasters. This chapter proposes the Ethical Governance Framework for Sustainable Tourism Resilience (EGF-STR). Drawing on Situational Crisis Communication Theory, Tourism Resilience Theory, Stakeholder Theory, and Institutional Theory, the framework explains how deepfake disaster communication contributes to information disorder, trust erosion, and tourism vulnerability. It incorporates proactive, adaptive, restorative, and sustainable governance mechanism to strengthen information integrity and ethical AI governance. The chapter provides a roadmap for resilience in an AI-driven environment

The microgrid (MG) operators face significant challenges in effectively meeting power demand requirements, considering the power distribution network&s;s limitations. Furthermore, the MG can use renewable energy (RE) sources to meet the demand response (DR) for customers&s; varying power needs, thereby reducing the carbon footprint. DR schemes provide operative solutions for several power system difficulties, including elevated generation costs, demand ratio, increased carbon footprint, reliability concerns, and overload in generation, transmission, and distribution networks. Optimization uses artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to improve forecasting of future supply and demand within an MG, which results in a more precise, on-time prediction of energy demand (ED) and supply changes. AI-managed, hyper-localized power grids could efficiently manage the intricate needs of a modern energy system consisting of innovative parts like time-varying prices and reliable renewable generation. The present chapter aims to understand the consequences of different perceptions in standalone MG areas. Due to the rising ED and depletion of traditional energy sources and the environmental issues involved in using fossil fuels, there has been an extensive use of RE resources around the world.

The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.

Anonymised questionnaire data (1049 entered records with screening flags), data dictionary, duplicate-screening script and list of excluded duplicate record pairs for the validation study of the Dependence on Artificial Intelligence scale and a compulsive ChatGPT use scale in 811 Tunisian university students (Solmi, Dergaa MA, Chalghaf, Dergaa I, Barakat, Alsaeed, Ahmetov and Jarraya).

Phishing and social engineering remain the main routes to fraud against bank customers. Static warnings lose force as users habituate to them. This paper presents APUX-Bank. This paper is a synthetic benchmark for the design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience (UX) models that defend bank customers against phishing. The dataset simulates a four-arm randomized experiment with 2,400 U.S. adult bank customers and 28,800 message decisions across email, SMS, voice and in-app channels. The four arms are a static warning, a rule-based adaptive warning, an AI-adaptive warning and an AI-adaptive warning with an explanation (AI-XAI). The data were generated from a seeded hierarchical logistic model. Its parameters were set from published phishing research. Logistic regression with participant-clustered errors showed that the AI-adaptive design reduced the odds of clicking a phishing message by 48 percent (OR = 0.52, 95% CI [0.45, 0.59]). The AI-XAI design reduced the odds by 56 percent (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.39, 0.51]). The benefit was largest for customers with low digital literacy. AI-XAI also raised usability by 6.2 points on the System Usability Scale and lowered false alarms. Trust in the system mediated 41 percent of its effect on phishing reports. The results held across GEE, random-intercept, probit and linear probability models. A parameter recovery test found that 29 of 31 true values fell inside their 95 percent confidence intervals. The data and all Python code are released for teaching, power analysis and method testing Keywords: Phishing, Social Engineering, Adaptive User Experience, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Banking Security, Synthetic Data, Logistic Regression.

Abstract Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is commonly associated with cognitive impairments and psychosocial difficulties that significantly affect quality of life beyond seizure burden. Individuals with DRE frequently experience difficulties in attention, memory, executive functioning, emotional regulation, stress, stigma, and social participation. Despite the high prevalence of these comorbidities, integrated rehabilitation approaches addressing both neurocognitive and psychosocial domains remain limited, particularly in resource-limited clinical settings. This article aims to develop and evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a structured neurocognitive and psychosocial intervention module for individuals with DRE. A multidisciplinary intervention module integrating psychoeducation, cognitive retraining exercises, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and family counseling was developed through literature review, clinical observations, and expert feedback. The intervention was delivered in eight weekly group sessions in Hindi and English at a tertiary neurology center in India. Ten adults with DRE participated in the pilot study. Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, attendance, adherence to home-based activities, and participant engagement. Acceptability was assessed through structured participant feedback regarding clarity, usefulness, relevance, and overall satisfaction with the intervention. Nine of 10 participants completed the intervention. Attendance, engagement, and adherence to home-based activities were satisfactory among participants who completed the study. Participants reported that the intervention content was understandable, relevant, and useful in daily functioning. Cognitive retraining exercises and CBT sessions were perceived as beneficial for improving coping, emotional regulation, and cognitive engagement. Family counseling sessions were positively received and were considered helpful in improving caregiver understanding and family support. One participant reported anxiety related to task performance during cognitive exercises. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of a structured neurocognitive and psychosocial intervention module for individuals with DRE within a tertiary care clinical setting. Further randomized controlled studies are underway to evaluate the clinical efficacy and long-term applicability of the intervention.

Abstract Background Large Language Models have become impactful in medicine by facilitating the processing of difficult medical data and aiding diagnosis-making. Given general LLM’s weaknesses, specialized medical LLMs are constructed for clinical precision, contextual understanding and safety in risky diagnostic applications. This review summarizes recent trends in medical LLMs for diagnosis, reported during 2021–2025. Methods A systematic literature review was performed following the PRISMA methodology. A search was designed and systematically carried out in the SCOPUS database using criteria of inclusion and exclusion (type of publication, language, period and country) and 75 peer-reviewed articles were chosen from a database of 1,911 records, after a multi-stage screening and eligibility evaluation. Results In summary, there have been significant advancements in the design and application of medical LLMs, with trends in hybrid architecture, multi-modal learning, prompt optimization techniques, diffusion-based imaging models, and multi-agent diagnostic system models. However, a number of persistent challenges that need to be overcome remain in the development and implementation of these models; namely, hallucination, bias, and poor probability calibration in LLMs, issues with explainability of LLMs, and ineffectiveness in a clinical environment. Conclusions This review highlights the fast pace of development and limitations of domain-specific medical LLMs. While impressive improvements in diagnostic performance have been made, the future directions must address improvements in reliability, safety and clinical validation in order to be seamlessly and responsibly incorporated in the practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The accelerating pace of urbanization has intensified demands on energy, water, transportation, and waste management systems, necessitating intelligent solutions that are both effective and environmentally sustainable. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated significant potential in optimizing urban operations; however, the increasing computational complexity and energy consumption of AI models pose new sustainability challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Green AI methodologies and introduces the Green AI Urban Framework (GAUF), a structured conceptual framework for integrating environmentally responsible AI into sustainable urban systems. The survey examines recent advances in energy-efficient model design, lightweight and adaptive learning techniques, data-efficient training, and resource-aware deployment strategies. Major urban application domains, including electricity demand prediction, water resource optimization, waste management, and smart mobility, are analyzed to identify current capabilities, limitations, and research gaps. Building on these insights, GAUF integrates three core components: sustainability-aware model selection, cloud–edge deployment strategies, and energy-efficiency evaluation metrics across the AI lifecycle. The framework also incorporates implementation and governance considerations relevant to urban infrastructure, sustainability reporting, and municipal adoption. GAUF aims to support researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in designing AI-driven urban systems that balance predictive performance, scalability, and environmental responsibility. By consolidating existing research and outlining future research directions, this study contributes to the development of sustainable AI practices as a core component of next-generation smart and resilient cities.
